passage:
Monday: Nikita and her friends planned to bunk the last period and go to the mall food court. "You're coming, Sharmila, right?" Sharmila laughed and said, "Maybe," though her stomach dropped.
Wednesday: She went. She spent the whole afternoon looking at her phone, expecting a call from school. The food tasted of nothing.
The next Monday: When they planned it again, Sharmila said, "I'm out. It's not my thing." Nikita rolled her eyes. "Boring." Sharmila shrugged, though her hands were cold. Two days later Nikita sat next to her in the library and asked quietly how she'd said no so easily. "It wasn't easy," Sharmila said.

qa.q: Where did the group go when they bunked?
qa.a: To the mall food court.

qa.q: Why did the food taste of nothing to Sharmila?
qa.a: She was anxious about being caught and uncomfortable doing something that didn't feel like her.

qa.q: What helped Sharmila say no the second time?
qa.a: She had already felt how wrong it was for her, so she could name it simply: "It's not my thing."

qa.q: What does Nikita's question in the library suggest about her?
qa.a: She may feel the pressure too and quietly admire Sharmila for resisting it.

grounding: It shows a teenager going along with group pressure once, then choosing to act as herself.

passage: Nilesh, I'll tell you about the worst day of my Class 11. My friends decided to make fun of a boy who stammered. They wanted me to imitate him during break, because I was good at voices. Everyone was waiting. "Come on, Manoj." My mouth went dry. I wanted to be the funny one; I also knew it was cruel. I said, "Not this," and walked off to the canteen. For a week they called me boring and didn't save me a seat. I ate alone. But on the fourth day the boy found me there and sat down without a word. We're still friends. I don't regret losing that seat.

qa.q: What did the friends want young Manoj to do?
qa.a: Imitate a boy who stammered during break.

qa.q: What was young Manoj feeling when his mouth went dry?
qa.a: Torn between wanting to be the funny one his friends admired and knowing the joke was cruel.

qa.q: What does Manoj's story show about the cost of standing firm?
qa.a: There can be a real price, like a week of eating alone, but it can also bring truer friendships.

qa.q: How might the boy who stammered have felt when he sat beside Manoj?
qa.a: Grateful and safe, recognising someone who had refused to mock him.

grounding: It shows, told by an elder, a teenager choosing their own values over intense pressure to go along with the group.

passage: It was eleven at night before the chemistry board exam, and the group video call was buzzing. Jatin said someone had "the paper" and was sharing a link. "Everyone's doing it, Rashmi. Don't be stupid." Rashmi's heart was pounding. She was tired, the power had just gone off, and her notes were half-revised by torchlight. Part of her wanted the link just to stop feeling behind. But she thought about the version of herself she liked: the one who earned her marks. "I'm going to sleep," she said. "Good luck." She left the call, set her alarm for five and revised by candlelight in the morning. The "paper" turned out to be fake. Half the call had studied the wrong questions.

qa.q: When was the group call?
qa.a: At eleven at night, before the chemistry board exam.

qa.q: Why was Rashmi tempted by the link?
qa.a: She was tired, behind in revision and the power had gone, so the link promised relief from feeling unprepared.

qa.q: What helped Rashmi resist the pressure?
qa.a: She thought about the kind of person she wanted to be and left the call, then used a practical plan of an early alarm.

qa.q: How might Jatin and the others feel the next day?
qa.a: Panicked and regretful, having wasted time on a fake paper while Rashmi revised.

grounding: It shows a teenager holding on to her own values against strong peer pressure at a stressful moment.

passage: The whole gang in Samir's colony in Hyderabad got the same buzz cut the week before term started. 'Your turn tomorrow,' they told him at the gate. Samir, fifteen, had been growing his curls since summer; he liked tying them back when he played the tabla. That night he stood in front of the mirror, pulling the curls straight, trying to picture himself without them. His neighbour Kashish, sixteen, out walking her dog, saw him on the steps later. 'You look like someone going to a punishment.' 'They're all doing it.' 'Do you want to?' He took a long time to answer. 'I want them to stop calling me the different one.' Next morning he went to the barber, asked for just a trim, and walked to the gate with his heart thumping.

qa.q: What instrument does Samir play?
qa.a: He plays the tabla.

qa.q: What did Samir's answer to Kashish show about what he wanted?
qa.a: He didn't want the haircut itself; he wanted to stop being singled out, so he felt torn between belonging and staying himself.

qa.q: What could help Samir if the group teases him about the trim?
qa.a: He could answer lightly and confidently, and spend time with people like Kashish who accept him as he is.

qa.q: What would change if Samir's friends had treated the haircut as optional?
qa.a: He could keep his curls without feeling he was risking his place in the group.

grounding: Shows a teenager torn between keeping his own look and matching his friends, and choosing his own way.

passage:
'Rajni, the group decided. Black dresses, all nine of us, for the farewell photo.'
'I heard.' Rajni kept folding Nani's green saree on the bed.
Mumma, from the doorway: 'That's the one you wanted to wear, na?'
'Wanted.'
Vandana sat down beside her. 'You'll look like the odd one out in the photo.'
'I know.'
'So?'
'So I've been thinking about it for three days.' Rajni ran her thumb along the border. 'Nani wore this to her own farewell. I wanted to wear it to mine.'
Mumma said nothing, which Rajni knew was deliberate.
Vandana sighed. 'What if you wear it for the function and change for the group photo?'
'That's... not bad.' Rajni looked up. 'Or I wear it the whole time and stand in the middle.'
Vandana laughed. 'Okay, bold. I'll stand next to you.'

qa.q: Who wore the green saree to her own farewell?
qa.a: Nani wore it to her own farewell.

qa.q: What does Rajni running her thumb along the border suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she feels torn, deeply attached to the saree and to Nani yet pulled by the wish to fit in with the group.

qa.q: How did Mumma support Rajni in this scene?
qa.a: She reminded her of what she had wanted and then stayed quiet, leaving the decision to Rajni.

qa.q: How does Vandana's view change during the talk?
qa.a: She starts by warning Rajni she will stand out, then offers a compromise and finally chooses to stand beside her.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager weighing her own wish against her group's plan to match, with her friend and mother present.

passage: I'm Devika. In Class 10 my whole group chose science. Everyone assumed I would too. I love history, the old maps, the stories behind the dates, but I didn't say anything for weeks. At lunch they'd plan who would sit together in physics. I nodded along. My friend Ishita finally asked, "Why do you look sad every time we talk about this?" I told her. She didn't laugh. She said, "Then pick history. I'll still sit with you at lunch." I did. Some of the others stopped inviting me. Ishita didn't. I still think about how close I came to choosing their future instead of mine.

qa.q: What subject does Devika love?
qa.a: History.

qa.q: How did Devika feel while nodding along to the science plans?
qa.a: Devika felt sad and trapped, hiding what she really wanted to fit in.

qa.q: What would you advise someone in Devika's position?
qa.a: Talk to one trusted friend or adult early, as Devika eventually did with Ishita.

qa.q: How might Ishita have felt watching Devika during those weeks?
qa.a: Concerned and puzzled, sensing something was wrong behind the nodding.

grounding: Shows a teenager choosing a personal path over the pressure to follow friends' subject choices.

passage:
Football coach's note, Sachin, September
On Friday, several boys from the team planned to skip the last class to go to the mall. Ojas (15) was invited and, I'm told, called "boring" when he said no. He came to practice instead, a little quiet. When I asked, he said, "I didn't want to, but I also didn't want to be left out." He made a good choice, and I told him so privately. I've also reminded the whole team about skipping classes. I'll pair Ojas with some of the senior players for drills.

qa.q: Where did the boys plan to go?
qa.a: To the mall.

qa.q: What was Ojas feeling at practice after saying no?
qa.a: He felt torn and a bit left out, even though he knew he'd made the choice he wanted.

qa.q: Why did Sachin pair Ojas with the senior players?
qa.a: To give him support and a sense of belonging for sticking with his choice.

qa.q: How might the boys who called him "boring" see Ojas later?
qa.a: They might respect him more if he doesn't back down, or keep teasing for a while.

grounding: Shows a teenager balancing his own values against peer pressure to skip class, noted by his coach.

passage:
Madhuri's diary, Sunday
Everyone in our group cut their hair the same way this week, short and layered. Keerthana said, "You'll look so good, just do it." I almost did. I sat in the salon chair and then said, "Just a trim." I like my long hair. I like my plait. At school tomorrow Keerthana will probably say I'm not part of the look. My stomach hurts a bit thinking about it. But I kept thinking: if I change something I love just to match, what's next? I'm fourteen. I want to figure out what I like before everyone decides for me.

qa.q: What haircut did the group get?
qa.a: Short and layered.

qa.q: How is Madhuri feeling about going to school tomorrow?
qa.a: Madhuri feels nervous and a little anxious about Keerthana's reaction.

qa.q: What would you advise Madhuri if Keerthana teases about the plait?
qa.a: Stay calm, say plainly that Madhuri likes the plait, and remember a good friend will accept that.

qa.q: How might Keerthana see Madhuri's choice?
qa.a: Keerthana might feel disappointed that Madhuri didn't match the group, or quietly respect the choice.

grounding: Shows a young teenager balancing personal taste against pressure to match friends' haircuts.

passage: In Mandya, Hemant, fifteen, went to classical singing class every Saturday. His friends laughed about it. "Arre, Pandit Hemant!" Chinmay would say. This Saturday Chinmay turned up at his door. "New film at the talkies. Everyone's going. Skip your aa-aa-aa." Hemant looked at his harmonium case. He thought of the group sitting together in the dark, laughing, and of Monday, when they'd talk about the film and he'd be quiet. "Come on," Chinmay said. "Or are you too cultured for us?" Hemant's jaw tightened. "I'll come next week. Today I have a raga to finish." Chinmay rolled his eyes and left. Hemant sat down with the harmonium, and it took a while before his fingers stopped shaking.

qa.q: What case did Hemant look at?
qa.a: His harmonium case.

qa.q: What was Hemant feeling when his jaw tightened?
qa.a: He felt stung and pressured by Chinmay's teasing, but determined to keep to his singing.

qa.q: How could Hemant stay close to his friends while keeping his singing?
qa.a: He could plan the film with them next week and invite them to hear him sing sometime.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Hemant's refusal?
qa.a: Chinmay may feel annoyed or rejected, seeing it as Hemant putting himself above the group.

grounding: A small-town teenager resists pressure to skip his singing class for a group film outing.

passage: In Seville, Diego, sixteen, had two things on Thursday afternoon: the chess club and football at the park with Gabriel's crowd. Everyone knew which one was cool. At lunch Gabriel threw an arm around his shoulder. "You're coming, right? We need a goalkeeper." Diego liked Gabriel. He liked being wanted. But the chess tournament was in three weeks and he'd been thinking about openings all morning. "I've got chess," he said. Gabriel laughed. "Chess? With the kids in cardigans?" A few boys laughed too. Diego felt heat in his face. He almost said, "Okay, I'll come." Instead he said, "Next week I'll play keeper." That afternoon, playing chess, he lost his first game. He still stayed till the end.

qa.q: When was the chess tournament?
qa.a: In three weeks.

qa.q: What was Diego feeling when the boys laughed?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and tempted to give in, torn between wanting Gabriel's approval and his love of chess.

qa.q: What could Diego do if the teasing continues?
qa.a: He could keep joining football sometimes, while standing firm on chess days, and talk honestly with Gabriel.

qa.q: How might Gabriel see Diego choosing chess?
qa.a: Gabriel might feel a little let down, but could respect that Diego knows what he wants.

grounding: A Spanish teenager chooses his chess club over football with a popular group despite teasing.

passage:
The Class 12 commerce classroom went quiet when Dilnaz said it.
"I'm not bunking tomorrow."
The plan had been made on the group chat: everyone would skip the extra accounts class and go to the new café. Vishal had already drafted the excuse message.
"Come on," he said. "If you come to class alone, sir will know something's up."
"Then he'll know. I need the class. I'm bad at accounts."
Someone muttered "topper behaviour." Dilnaz's ears went red. She picked at her eraser and nearly said fine, she'd come.
Vishal looked at her for a long moment. "Actually, I'm bad at accounts too," he said. "Maybe I'll come."
Next day four of them sat in the class. The café could wait for Saturday.

qa.q: What did Vishal already draft?
qa.a: The excuse message.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz feel when someone muttered "topper behaviour"?
qa.a: She felt embarrassed and pressured; her ears went red and she nearly gave in.

qa.q: What helped Dilnaz stay true to her choice, and what could help her next time?
qa.a: Stating her real reason simply helped; next time she could suggest a Saturday plan so she stays close to the group without skipping class.

qa.q: How might Vishal have seen Dilnaz's stand?
qa.a: Vishal may have respected her honesty and felt relieved to admit he was also weak at accounts.

grounding: Shows a student holding her own choice against strong group pressure, and how it shifts others.

passage:
Dear Omkar,
You'll laugh, but I need to tell someone who doesn't go to my school.
Everyone in my class has started wearing their hair the same way, straightened and flat. I've always loved my curls. Last Friday a girl I like said, "You'd look so much older with it straight." On Saturday I stood in the salon for ten minutes and walked out without going in.
Part of me wanted to fit in so badly my chest hurt. Part of me was angry that I even wanted it.
On Monday I wore my curls with a new clip. Two girls said it looked nice. One rolled her eyes. I survived both.
I'm still not sure I made the "right" choice. But I'm glad it was mine.
Mehak

qa.q: How long did Mehak stand in the salon?
qa.a: Ten minutes, then walked out without going in.

qa.q: What was Mehak feeling outside the salon?
qa.a: Mehak felt torn: wanting to fit in so badly the chest hurt, and angry at wanting it.

qa.q: What would you advise a friend in Mehak's place?
qa.a: Take time, as Mehak did, and choose what feels like your own, knowing some people will like it and some won't.

qa.q: How might Omkar feel reading this letter from outside her school?
qa.a: Omkar may feel trusted and proud of Mehak, and able to see the pressure more calmly from outside that school.

grounding: A teen's letter weighing the wish to conform against keeping her own style.

passage:
So you want the story for the school podcast, Yusuf? Fine. I'm Ramesh, Class 11, and last year I nearly got a tattoo I didn't want.
My whole cricket team decided to get the same small bat tattoo on the wrist after we won the district trophy. I love the team. But the idea of a needle, and of my father's face, made me sick.
Everyone kept saying, "Don't be the one who ruins it." I booked the appointment anyway. I sat in the waiting chair and my hands were shaking.
Then I stood up, went back out and bought the team matching wristbands instead. I told them, "Same bat, no needle." Two of them switched too.
I still wear mine at every match.

qa.q: What did Ramesh buy instead of the tattoo?
qa.a: Matching wristbands for the team.

qa.q: How can you tell Ramesh was anxious in the waiting chair?
qa.a: Ramesh's hands were shaking, which shows fear and pressure.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and why?
qa.a: Buying wristbands worked because Ramesh stayed loyal to the team without doing something Ramesh did not want.

qa.q: How might the teammates who switched to wristbands have felt?
qa.a: They may have felt relieved, as if someone finally gave them permission to say no.

grounding: A teen speaks about resisting team pressure while still honouring belonging.

passage: I'm Pankaj, in Himani's section. On Thursday the class group decided on a mass bunk for Friday's last two periods, to go and see a film. Everyone reacted with thumbs-ups. Himani didn't reply for an hour. Then she wrote, "I've got band practice, you guys go." Someone replied "boring 🙄" and a couple of people laughed at it. At lunch on Friday I saw her sitting a bit apart, fiddling with her drumsticks, not really eating. But when the bell rang, she walked to the music room, not the gate. I went with the others. I don't know if she regretted it. She was smiling when I passed the music room window, though.

qa.q: What reason did Himani give for not joining the bunk?
qa.a: She had band practice.

qa.q: What does Himani fiddling with her drumsticks at lunch suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt uneasy and a little left out after the "boring" comment, even though she had decided.

qa.q: What could help Himani hold her choice without feeling isolated?
qa.a: She could spend time with band friends who share her interest, and remind herself why practice matters to her.

qa.q: How does Pankaj see Himani's choice?
qa.a: Pankaj notices her unease but also her smile, unsure whether she regretted it, while going along with the others.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager choosing her own commitment over a class bunk despite teasing, seen by a classmate.
